CHAPTER 9: RELIGION AS A SOURCE OF COMMUNAL VALUES

LEARNING OUTCOMES
- Outline the relationship between the understanding of the transcendent/God and the concept of the person in two religious traditions.
- Give two examples of how these connections decide behavioural norms (rules for how people behave) in religious traditions.
- The two traditions studied in this chapter are Judaism and Christianity.

KEY TERMS
- Concept of God: the understanding of the nature of God in a particular world religion.
- Covenant: a contract or agreement between people (as in marriage), or between one or more people and God. In the Old Testament, God made covenants with Noah, Abraham and Moses.
- Stewardship: supervising or taking care of something, for example the environment.
- Incarnation: when the Second Person of the Holy Trinity took on our human nature, taking flesh in the womb of the Virgin Mary. (God became part of human history in the person of Jesus.)
- Monotheistic religion: a religion that believes in one God. Christianity and Judaism are two of the major monotheistic world religions.
- Shabbat: the Hebrew word for the Sabbath.
- Seder meal: the special Passover meal held in the home.
- Matzah: unleavened bread eaten at the Seder meal.
- Haggadah: the story of the Exodus, read at the Seder meal.
- Messiah: the saviour God promised to send. Jewish people still await him.
- Paradoxical: contradictory (seeming to say two opposite things at once).
- Presupposes: assumes.

INDIVIDUAL WORK: VALUES AND BEHAVIOUR (opening activity)
- Students think about how their values affect how they behave in school, at home, with friends and in a church or place of worship.
- They ask what is the biggest influence on their behaviour and link it to their values.

INTRODUCTION
- The title of the book (The Search for Meaning and Values) presupposes (assumes) that meaning and values exist and that humans have always searched for both.
- Earlier chapters showed that the search for meaning is part of what it means to be human - it is part of our nature.
- The search is expressed in contemporary culture and in ancient cultures. Myth, philosophy and science have all contributed to it.
- Religion tries to answer life's great questions from a particular perspective.
- Chapter 8 explored the concept of God as it emerged in human history. Understanding God and God's relationship with humans is central to a religious response to life's great questions.
- Key questions: How does our understanding of God shape how we understand ourselves and our world? How does this self-understanding affect how we live?
- From a religious point of view, the search for meaning and values leads us into the realm of the sacred or transcendent.
- Religion uses symbols and rituals to help people name key moments and events.
- Religion encourages people to gather together and discover the meaning and values to live by.
- Quote: 'The hearts of Men should seek beyond the world and should find no rest therein.' - J. R. R. Tolkien.
- Each religion has its own focus, rituals and beliefs, but all share a belief in God or a divine being. This belief is central to how each religion answers life's key questions.
- Example: when Christians experience death, they respond with a belief in an afterlife.

RELIGION AS A SOURCE OF COMMUNAL VALUES
- Two major monotheistic world religions: Christianity and Judaism.
- The concept of God is different in each. Each understanding of God and of God's relationship with humanity has led to different understandings of the individual and of what counts as right living.
- The chapter focuses on one central image or concept of God in each tradition and how it has shaped the understanding of the person.

GOD AND THE PERSON IN JUDAISM
- Two key sources: the creation accounts in Hebrew scripture (Genesis) and the story of the Exodus of the Jewish people from Egypt.
- The concept of God in Hebrew scripture directly affects how Jewish people see themselves as God's people, and so affects how they live.
- Other books that throw light on the Jewish understanding of God: the Psalms, the book of Proverbs, the books of the prophets and the book of Job.

THE FIRST CREATION ACCOUNT (GENESIS 1)
- Found at the start of Genesis (Genesis 1:1). It tells of the seven days of creation.
- God created humans on the sixth day.
- Quote: 'Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness; and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea... So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.' God told them, 'Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it'.
- Meaning: God created humanity in his image. Of all creation, humans are unique in their likeness to God, and they have dominion (rule) over all of creation.
- Context: written when the people of Israel were in exile in Babylon. They may have felt abandoned by God and despaired about their future.
- The account reminded them that God is powerful. God created order and light out of chaos and darkness.
- Most importantly, God created humanity, and humanity is in relationship with God.

THE SECOND CREATION ACCOUNT (GENESIS 2:4 - 3:24)
- It is actually much older than the first account.
- Scholars agree its purpose is not to give a historical or detailed account of creation, but to remind people of their relationship to God.
- It tells of the creation of humanity, in which male and female are equal.
- It also tells of the 'fall': humanity becomes estranged (separated) from God because of the actions of Adam and Eve.
- This paradoxical (contradictory) situation - being both loved by God and estranged from God - shapes how believers understand themselves.

GOD'S PROMISE OF A SAVIOUR
- Even though humans turned away from God, God promised he would still be their God and would one day send a saviour to redeem them.
- Jewish people still await this saviour (the Messiah).
- At the Seder meal at Passover, Jewish people leave one empty seat at the table for the prophet Elijah, hoping he will announce the coming of the Messiah - the fulfilment of God's promise made from the beginning.
- There is a special and intimate relationship between God and humanity. Jewish people see themselves as God's chosen people.

DISTANCE BETWEEN GOD AND HUMANITY
- Alongside the special relationship, there is an acknowledgement of distance between God and humans.
- A dominant theme of Hebrew scripture: nobody has ever seen the face of God.
- Possible reasons: (1) humanity cannot understand the wonder of God; (2) the first estrangement caused by Adam and Eve - because of sin, humanity is not worthy to see God's face.
- Consequence: the worship of idols or images is prohibited. Judaism is monotheistic, and together with the belief that no one could see God's face, there is a strict rule against idol worship.
- Summary from Genesis: God created humanity and set humans apart from the rest of creation; humanity also became estranged from God.

JUDAISM EXAMPLE 1: THE SABBATH
- Based on Genesis 1:27: 'God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them, male and female he created them.'
- Because they are made in God's image, Jewish people keep a special relationship with God through prayer and worship.
- They worship in the synagogue on the Sabbath (Hebrew: Shabbat), on Friday evening and Saturday morning.
- The Sabbath is a weekly chance to praise and thank God for all their blessings.
- It is a time to retreat from the daily cycle of life, to worship and pray, and to focus on family.
- This comes from seeing God as their creator and themselves as people created by him in a special relationship.

JUDAISM EXAMPLE 2: FALSE IDOLS
- Traditionally, Jewish people do not say God's name aloud and do not display images of God in the synagogue.
- This is because the Ten Commandments forbid worshipping idols.
- Quote (Exodus 20:2-5): 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself an idol... You shall not bow down to them or worship them.'
- Jewish people are faithful to the commandments, and the way they worship reflects this.
- These examples show the concept of God affects the understanding of the person, which in turn affects how Jewish people behave.

THE EXODUS ACCOUNT AND COVENANT
- The Exodus became the central event in the Jewish celebration of Passover.
- God was faithful and kept his promises, and he expected the same faithfulness in return.
- Covenant is at the heart of Judaism. It expresses a unique bond between God and his people.
- The covenant of Mount Sinai made the Ten Commandments central to everything Jewish people do.
- From the covenant comes a strong adherence (sticking) to the commandments and the golden rule as outlined in the scriptures.
- Jewish people saw themselves as people who had promised God to live as he asked.
- Image of God as LAWGIVER: this leads to huge respect for every detail of the Law, and Jewish people keep these laws in daily life.
- Examples of keeping the Law: attending the synagogue weekly; following Kosher laws when preparing and eating food; wearing a prayer shawl during prayer with 613 tassels, one for each Law of the Torah.
- Through Moses, God called the people of Israel and led them out of slavery into the Promised Land.
- As part of the covenant, Jewish people stayed faithful to the Law and in worship they remember their liberation. Passover is central to this and is celebrated every year.

JUDAISM EXAMPLE: PASSOVER
- A festival lasting eight days. It celebrates the Jewish people's delivery from slavery in Egypt.
- The Seder meal is a special meal held in the home.
- At the Seder, matzah (unleavened bread) is eaten and the Haggadah (the story of the Exodus) is read.
- The story teaches the next generation how Jewish people understand themselves as a people liberated by God.
- Quote: 'Let all who are hungry come and eat.' - Passover Haggadah.

CONCLUSION ON JUDAISM
- The concept of God affects the behaviour of Jewish people.
- This can be seen in their fidelity (faithfulness) to the Law, their attitude to the land of Israel, and their worship.

SUMMARY - JUDAISM
- The creation accounts in Genesis are important sources for the Jewish concept of God.
- They reveal God as CREATOR of humanity, so Jewish people understand themselves as created by God.
- So they have a special relationship with God and their behaviour should reflect this.
- The Exodus account reveals God as LIBERATOR, so a Jewish person understands themselves as liberated by God.
- As a result, Jewish people show gratitude to God by being faithful to the commands of the Torah and through worship.

GOD AND THE PERSON IN CHRISTIANITY: THE CREATION ACCOUNTS
- Christianity draws on the same creation accounts as Judaism. The Christian Old Testament contains many books of the Hebrew scriptures; the two religions share a common heritage.
- For Christians, the creator God of Genesis is the same God revealed through Jesus in the New Testament.
- The creation accounts show God is the creator of the universe.
- Because God created the world in all its beauty and diversity, Christianity promotes a spirituality that holds all of God's creation in high regard - a 'world-affirming spirituality', seen in early Christian writings.

CHRISTIANITY EXAMPLE 1: STEWARDSHIP OF THE EARTH
- In the Christian understanding of creation, humans are given the special task of caring for creation. This is also true of Judaism and Islam.
- Because humans have a special role and relationship with God, they are expected to care for the earth.
- Creation is not ours - it is entrusted to us by God. Humans are the high point of creation but have also been given a huge responsibility.
- The ecological and environmental implications are vast. If it matters to God how humans treat the earth, failing to care for it could be seen as sinful.
- There is a new awareness of this responsibility because of regular ecological catastrophes today (e.g. forest fires caused by global warming).
- Pope Francis' encyclical Laudato si' (On Care for Our Common Home), released in 2015, appeals to all humanity to care for the earth and change our way of life to repair the damage to the ecosystem.
- For Christians, the creation accounts show God created humans to be in relationship with God. This relationship is fundamental; without it humanity will not reach its true potential.
- Quote: 'You made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they find their rest in you.' - St Augustine of Hippo.
- The God of the creation accounts is a loving God who created a beautiful world and placed it in humanity's care.
- God's creation of and love for humanity means Christians are called to recognise the sacredness of human life.
- Christian groups and people dedicated to stewardship: Trócaire (an organisation); Fr Sean McDonagh, a Columban priest and ecologist.
- This behaviour is inspired by the Christian concept of God as creator and the understanding of themselves as stewards of creation.

CHRISTIANITY EXAMPLE 2: GOD REVEALED THROUGH JESUS CHRIST
- For Christians, God is revealed in a unique way through Jesus Christ. God, who until then had been invisible, is made visible and known through Jesus.
- The life, death and resurrection of Jesus are the foundational events of Christianity.
- Doctrine of the Incarnation: the belief that God became part of human history in the person of Jesus. It is central to the Christian understanding of God and humanity.
- Colossians 1:15: Jesus is 'the image of the invisible God'.
- John 14:9: 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.'
- Through Jesus, humanity was forgiven and redeemed. His death and resurrection revealed God's unconditional love for humanity.
- The life of Jesus shows his followers how to live. Jesus preached a world where mercy ruled justice, where the outcast were loved, and where love of God was the centre of life.
- Jesus called people to choose peace over violence, to include rather than exclude, and to share rather than hoard.
- He based all this on seeing God as loving, forgiving and closely involved in the world.
- John 15:13: 'No one has a greater love than the one who lays down his life for others.' Jesus laid down his life out of love for humanity.
- Main implication: in all areas of life, Christians are called to live as Jesus did.

CHRISTIANITY EXAMPLE 3: LIVING CHRISTIAN LIVES
- Christians aim to live as Jesus did.
- The law of love is the ultimate guide for all Christian moral living (Matthew 22:38-40): 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment and the second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as you love yourself.'
- Christians show mercy, forgiveness and love in how they live.
- Examples of people living Gospel values: Dr Martin Luther King, Mother Teresa and Pope Francis. (A Martin Luther King Jr memorial monument stands in Washington, DC.)
- You do not need to look to famous people - every day ordinary Christians live in a way inspired by their understanding of God and of themselves as followers of Jesus.

SUMMARY - CHRISTIANITY
- Christianity draws on the same creation accounts as Judaism.
- Like Judaism, God is revealed as creator of humanity; Christians are called to be in relationship with God and to recognise the sacredness of human life.
- God is revealed as creator of the earth, so Christians should be stewards of the earth and work hard to care for it.
- God is revealed in a unique way through Jesus Christ.
- God showed his unconditional love for humanity through the death and resurrection of Jesus.
- So Christians understand themselves as loved by God.
- Their lives should reflect this: they too should be loving, forgiving and merciful.

COMPARING THE TWO TRADITIONS (from the chapter)
- Both are monotheistic and share the Genesis creation accounts and a common heritage.
- Judaism: central images of God = Creator (Genesis) and Liberator/Lawgiver (Exodus, covenant at Sinai). Person = made in God's image, chosen, liberated, but also estranged; behaviour = Sabbath worship, no idols or saying God's name, keeping the Law (Kosher, synagogue, 613 tassels), Passover.
- Christianity: central images of God = Creator and God revealed in Jesus (Incarnation). Person = made for relationship with God, steward of creation, loved and redeemed; behaviour = caring for the earth (Laudato si', Trócaire, Fr Sean McDonagh), respecting the sacredness of life, living the law of love like Jesus (Martin Luther King, Mother Teresa, Pope Francis).

SAMPLE EXAM QUESTION AND TIP
- Sample question: 'Profile the connection between the understanding of the transcendent/God and how the human person is understood in the teaching of two of the above world religions' (Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism). (40 marks)
- Exam tip: use what you learned in earlier chapters about the concept of God and divine revelation in Christianity and Judaism, the emergence of monotheism, and the covenant with God.

rows.prompt: Define 'covenant' and name the three people God made covenants with in the Old Testament.
rows.model_answer: A covenant is a contract or agreement between people, such as marriage, or between one or more people and God. In the Old Testament, God made covenants with Noah, Abraham and Moses.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words what the first creation account in Genesis teaches about human beings.
rows.model_answer: It teaches that God created humans on the sixth day in his own image and likeness, male and female. Humans are unique among all creation in being like God and are given dominion over the rest of creation. Above all, it shows that humanity is in a relationship with God.

rows.prompt: Explain why Judaism has a strict rule against the worship of idols.
rows.model_answer: A dominant theme of Hebrew scripture is that no one has ever seen the face of God, either because humans cannot understand his wonder or because sin makes them unworthy. Judaism is also monotheistic. Together these beliefs mean images or idols of God are forbidden, as the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2-5) state.

rows.prompt: Describe how Jewish people keep the Sabbath and explain why.
rows.model_answer: Jewish people worship in the synagogue on Shabbat, Friday evening and Saturday morning. It is a weekly time to praise and thank God for their blessings, to step back from daily life, to pray and to focus on family. They do this because God is their creator and they were made in his image, so they have a special relationship with him.

rows.prompt: Name two ways Jewish people show respect for the Law in daily life.
rows.model_answer: They attend the synagogue weekly and follow Kosher laws when preparing and eating food. During prayer they also wear a prayer shawl with 613 tassels, one for each Law of the Torah. This comes from seeing God as lawgiver in the covenant at Mount Sinai.

rows.prompt: Describe the Seder meal.
rows.model_answer: The Seder is a special meal held in the home during Passover, an eight-day festival celebrating freedom from slavery in Egypt. Matzah (unleavened bread) is eaten and the Haggadah, the story of the Exodus, is read. An empty seat is left for the prophet Elijah.

rows.prompt: Explain what stewardship means for Christians and give one example of it in action.
rows.model_answer: Stewardship means caring for creation, which God has entrusted to humans; creation is not ours. Because humans have a special relationship with God, they are expected to care for the earth. For example, Pope Francis' encyclical Laudato si' (2015) calls all people to care for our common home, and Trócaire and Fr Sean McDonagh work to care for the earth.

rows.prompt: Explain the doctrine of the Incarnation and what it means for how Christians live.
rows.model_answer: The Incarnation is the belief that God became part of human history in Jesus; the invisible God is made visible through him (Colossians 1:15, John 14:9). Jesus' life, death and resurrection show God's unconditional love and forgiveness. So Christians are called to live as Jesus did - merciful, forgiving, peaceful, including others and sharing.

rows.prompt: What is the 'law of love' in Christianity?
rows.model_answer: The law of love is the ultimate guide for Christian moral living (Matthew 22:38-40). It is to love God with all your heart, soul and mind, and to love your neighbour as yourself.

rows.prompt: Outline how the Jewish understanding of God as creator influences how Jewish people understand themselves. Give one example of how this affects their behaviour.
rows.model_answer:
In Judaism, the creation accounts in Genesis reveal God as the creator of humanity. The first account (Genesis 1) says God created humans on the sixth day 'in his image... male and female he created them' and gave them dominion over creation. This shows humans are unique and set apart, and in a special relationship with God. Written during the exile in Babylon, it reminded the Israelites that God is powerful and had not abandoned them. The older second account (Genesis 2:4-3:24) shows male and female as equal, but also tells of the fall, where humanity became estranged from God through Adam and Eve. So Jewish people see themselves as both loved by God and distant from him. They also see themselves as God's chosen people.

This affects behaviour through the Sabbath (Shabbat). Because they are made in God's image, Jewish people keep their relationship with God through worship in the synagogue on Friday evening and Saturday morning. The Sabbath is a weekly time to praise and thank God for their blessings, to retreat from daily life, to pray and to focus on family.
rows.marking_scheme: Outline of understanding of the person: 6 marks (2 marks x 3 points, e.g. made in God's image; set apart with dominion; special/chosen relationship; loved yet estranged through the fall). Example of behaviour: 4 marks (name 1 + explain 3). Accept the Sabbath or the rule against idols/God's name.

rows.prompt: Explain how the Exodus and the covenant at Mount Sinai shape the way Jewish people live today. Refer to two examples.
rows.model_answer:
The Exodus reveals God as a liberator. Through Moses, God called the people of Israel and led them out of slavery in Egypt into the Promised Land. God was faithful to his promises and expected faithfulness in return. This is the idea of covenant, which is at the heart of Judaism and expresses a unique bond between God and his people. The covenant of Mount Sinai made the Ten Commandments central to everything Jewish people do. They see themselves as a people who promised God to live as he asked, and as a people liberated by God.

Because God is seen as lawgiver, Jewish people have great respect for every detail of the Law. For example, they attend the synagogue weekly, follow Kosher laws when preparing and eating food, and wear a prayer shawl with 613 tassels, one for each Law of the Torah. They also refuse to make images of God, following Exodus 20:2-5.

A second example is Passover, an eight-day festival celebrating delivery from slavery in Egypt. At the Seder meal in the home, matzah is eaten and the Haggadah is read, teaching the next generation that they are a people liberated by God. An empty seat is left for Elijah, who will announce the Messiah.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: God as liberator; Moses and slavery in Egypt; covenant as a unique bond; Mount Sinai and the Ten Commandments; God as lawgiver; synagogue, Kosher laws, prayer shawl with 613 tassels; no idols; Passover (eight days, Seder, matzah, Haggadah, Elijah's seat). Two examples must be developed for high marks.

rows.prompt: Explain the Christian idea of stewardship and show how it comes from the Christian concept of God. Refer to one organisation or person in your answer.
rows.model_answer:
Christianity shares the Genesis creation accounts with Judaism. For Christians, the creator God of Genesis is the same God revealed in Jesus. Because God created the world in all its beauty and diversity, Christianity has a world-affirming spirituality that holds all creation in high regard. God placed this beautiful world in the care of humanity.

Stewardship means taking care of something, such as the environment. Humans have a special role and relationship with God, so they are expected to care for the earth. Creation is not ours - it is entrusted to us by God. Humans are the high point of creation but also have a huge responsibility. If it matters to God how we treat the earth, failing to care for it could be seen as sinful. Today's regular ecological catastrophes, such as forest fires caused by global warming, have created a new awareness of this.

In 2015 Pope Francis released Laudato si' (On Care for Our Common Home), appealing to all humanity to care for the earth and to change our way of life to repair the damage to the ecosystem. Trócaire and the Columban priest and ecologist Fr Sean McDonagh are also dedicated to caring for the earth.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. May refer to: definition of stewardship; God as creator of a beautiful world; creation entrusted not owned; humans as high point with responsibility; failure as sinful; ecological catastrophes; Laudato si' (2015, Pope Francis); Trócaire; Fr Sean McDonagh. Must link stewardship to the concept of God for top band.

rows.prompt: Profile the connection between the understanding of God and how the human person is understood in the teaching of Judaism and Christianity.
rows.model_answer:
Judaism and Christianity are monotheistic and share the Genesis creation accounts. In both, God is creator and humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), unique in creation and in relationship with God.

In Judaism, the second account shows humanity estranged from God through Adam and Eve, so Jewish people see themselves as both loved and distant. No one has seen God's face, so idols are forbidden and God's name is not said aloud. Jewish people see themselves as God's chosen people. The Exodus reveals God as liberator and lawgiver; the covenant of Mount Sinai makes the Ten Commandments central. So Jewish people keep the Sabbath, follow Kosher laws, wear a prayer shawl with 613 tassels and celebrate Passover, reading the Haggadah to teach that they are a people liberated by God.

In Christianity, God as creator makes humans stewards of creation, which is entrusted to them (Laudato si', 2015). Humans are made for relationship with God: as St Augustine said, 'our hearts are restless until they find their rest in you.' Human life is sacred. God is revealed uniquely in Jesus through the Incarnation: Jesus is 'the image of the invisible God' (Colossians 1:15). His death and resurrection show God's unconditional love, so Christians see themselves as loved and redeemed. They live by the law of love (Matthew 22:38-40), as Martin Luther King, Mother Teresa and Pope Francis did.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Marks for each tradition roughly equal. Judaism may refer to: creator, image of God, chosen people, fall/estrangement, no one sees God's face, idols forbidden, liberator/lawgiver, covenant at Sinai, Sabbath, Kosher, 613 tassels, Passover. Christianity may refer to: shared creation accounts, stewardship, Laudato si', Augustine, sacredness of life, Incarnation, Colossians 1:15, John 14:9, unconditional love, law of love, named examples. Clear link between God and the person needed in each.
